welcome.transcript: Welcome to Eos, a museum where you can hear our changing planet. This museum has four exhibits, each turning NASA satellite data into music. You'll hear how city lights have changed, how oceans are warming, how carbon dioxide ebbs and flows, and where lightning strikes around the world. Each exhibit plays a short piece of music with a spoken explanation. Use the keyboard shortcuts or tab through the controls to explore. Enjoy your visit.

closing.transcript: Thank you for visiting Eos. Every sound you heard was shaped by real NASA data, measurements taken from satellites orbiting hundreds of miles above us, turned into music so you could hear what our planet is going through. I hope it gave you a new way to feel the changes happening on Earth. Safe travels.

exhibits.title: Earth's Night Lights, 2012–2023
exhibits.summary: Hear where city lights grew and faded over a decade.
exhibits.alt: NASA satellite map of Earth at night showing changes in city lights between 2012 and 2023. Purple areas show where lights increased; orange areas show where lights decreased.
exhibits.longDescription: A dark world map viewed from space showing how night lights changed between 2012 and 2023. Purple marks areas where lights increased — parts of India, Southeast Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa glow brighter than a decade ago as populations grew and economies expanded. Orange marks areas where lights decreased — regions in the Middle East and North Africa show dimmed patches where conflict or disaster disrupted infrastructure. Dense webs of stable light cover eastern North America, Europe, and East Asia.
exhibits.whatItShows: Satellite measurements of artificial light at night, comparing 2012 to 2023. Purple indicates areas where lights increased; orange indicates areas where lights decreased. The changes reveal where populations grew, where economies expanded, and where conflict or disaster reduced human activity.
soundRules: More voices join the choir where more light change is detected.
Higher-pitched voices represent areas with the most intense change.
The harmony shifts between major and minor chords as the balance of growth and decline changes across regions.
exhibits.data: NASA SVS: Change in Night Lights between 2012 and 2023
exhibits.transcript: Exhibit 1: Earth's Night Lights. You're looking at a map of every artificial light visible from space, comparing 2012 to 2023. In the music, each voice in the choir represents a region of the globe. Where lights grew brighter, more voices join and the pitch rises. Where lights dimmed, sometimes from conflict, sometimes from disaster, the harmony shifts to minor chords and the voice trembles. Listen for the contrast between the growing glow of India and the darkened patches over Syria. The music scans from west to east across the planet, so the choir builds as it passes through the most populated regions.

exhibits.title: Ocean Currents and Temperature
exhibits.summary: Listen to the ocean's currents and rising heat across the globe.
exhibits.alt: Global ocean surface currents and temperature visualization showing warm reds near the equator and cool blues near the poles, with flow lines tracing ocean currents.
exhibits.longDescription: A global map of ocean surface currents and temperatures rendered in a gradient from deep blue at the poles through green and yellow in temperate zones to vivid red and orange in the tropics. White dots and flow lines trace the direction of ocean currents. The warmest waters form a wide band along the equator, with tongues of warm water extending poleward along western boundary currents like the Gulf Stream and Kuroshio. Cool upwelling zones appear along the western coasts of continents.
exhibits.whatItShows: Ocean surface current directions and sea surface temperatures from the ECCO2 (Estimating the Circulation and Climate of the Ocean, Phase II) model. The visualization illustrates the flow of ocean currents using data points and interpolated flow curves, with color representing temperature — blue for cold polar waters through red for warm tropical waters.
soundRules: A deep bass drone represents the ocean's cold depths.
Flowing voices glide between notes like currents, breathing in slow swells.
A detuned shimmer enters where waters are warmest — beautiful but unsettling.
Bright sparkles mark the hottest surface temperatures.
exhibits.data: NASA SVS: ECCO2 Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature
exhibits.transcript: Exhibit 2: Ocean Temperatures. The ocean covers 70 percent of Earth's surface and has absorbed over 90 percent of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases. A deep bass drone represents the ocean's cold depths. Flowing voices glide between notes like currents, breathing in and out in slow swells. Where the water is warmer, a detuned second voice enters, creating a shimmer that's beautiful but unsettling. Bright sparkles mark the hottest surface temperatures. The piece scans from the cool Atlantic through the warm tropics to the vast Pacific. Notice how the warmth never really fades. The ocean remembers every degree.

exhibits.title: Carbon Dioxide, 2020
exhibits.summary: Hear the rhythm of CO₂ concentration in the atmosphere.
exhibits.alt: Atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration visualization showing swirling plumes of CO₂ over Earth's surface.
exhibits.longDescription: A view of Earth wrapped in translucent layers of color representing atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration during January through March 2020. Dense orange and red plumes hover over industrialized regions — eastern China, the eastern United States, and Europe. The gas visibly flows and swirls with atmospheric circulation, carried by jet streams across the Pacific and Atlantic.
exhibits.whatItShows: Carbon dioxide concentration simulated by the DYAMOND (DYnamics of the Atmospheric general circulation Modeled On Non-hydrostatic Domains) global model, showing January through March 2020. The visualization reveals the distribution of CO₂ across the atmosphere, with dense plumes over industrialized regions and the flow of carbon dioxide carried by atmospheric circulation patterns.
soundRules: A steady bass pulse represents the rhythm of CO₂ concentration across frames.
The lead tone only climbs — it never comes back down, accumulating like the gas itself.
The chords grow increasingly dissonant as concentration rises.
At the end, there is no resolution — the music simply stops, because the CO₂ doesn't.
exhibits.data: NASA SVS: DYAMOND Global Carbon Dioxide
exhibits.transcript: Exhibit 3: Carbon Dioxide. Every year, Earth breathes. In spring, forests pull carbon dioxide out of the air. In winter, they release it back. A steady bass pulse represents the seasonal cycle, Earth breathing in and out. But that pulse accelerates as concentration rises. The lead tone only climbs, it never comes back down, and each new high note stays, accumulating like the gas itself. The chords grow increasingly dissonant as we pass 400 parts per million. Taiko drums mark the highest concentration peaks. And at the end, there is no resolution. The music simply stops, because the CO₂ doesn't.

exhibits.title: Lightning, 2017–2023
exhibits.summary: Experience the flash and rumble of global lightning patterns.
exhibits.alt: Global lightning frequency map showing bright hotspots of electrical storm activity over tropical land masses.
exhibits.longDescription: A dark globe dotted with points of white and lavender light representing lightning strikes detected between March 2017 and July 2023. The densest clusters appear over tropical land masses — the Congo Basin in central Africa is the brightest spot on Earth, followed by northern South America and the Maritime Continent of Southeast Asia. Lightning over oceans is sparse. The pattern follows afternoon convection: heat from the sun warms land, driving thunderstorms that peak in local afternoon and evening hours.
exhibits.whatItShows: Lightning flash events detected by the Lightning Imaging Sensor (LIS) aboard the International Space Station between March 2017 and July 2023. Earth experiences roughly 45 lightning flashes per second. The data reveals that lightning is overwhelmingly a land phenomenon driven by solar heating, and its distribution is shifting as the climate warms.
soundRules: Percussive strikes represent individual lightning flashes.
The density of strikes matches the flash rate in each frame.
Low rumbling tones follow each cluster, simulating distant thunder.
Silence between flashes represents the dark sky — lightning is violent but brief.
exhibits.data: NASA SVS: Global Lightning Activity (LIS on ISS, March 2017 – July 2023)
exhibits.transcript: Exhibit 4: Lightning. Right now, roughly 45 bolts of lightning are striking the Earth every second. This piece maps where they fall. The piece begins in near silence, the dark sky between flashes. When lightning strikes, you hear an explosion: a taiko drum for thunder, a guitar stab for the bolt, and a rapid crackle of electrical energy that decays in milliseconds. Each flash comes from a different direction in the stereo field. The densest cluster is the Congo Basin, the single most electric place on Earth. Notice the silence between strikes. Lightning is violent but brief, and the darkness always returns.
